Tiago Almeida, co-author of ChatGPT and GPT-4, analyzes why RLHF models are structurally limited to human assistance and details how his new startup, TypeSafe, is rebuilding post-training for true automation.

## Overview

In this presentation, early OpenAI researcher Tiago Almeida addresses the stark divide currently split between two AI 'cults': one celebrating constant human-level benchmark breakthroughs, and another warning of an overhyped bubble of glorified chatbots. Almeida reconciles these views by separating LLM performance into two distinct goals: assistance and automation. AI is currently outstanding at assistance because the entire modern stack was built on RLHF, which explicitly puts a human in the loop and optimizes for human preference. However, this same mechanism makes current models fundamentally unsuited for autonomous, high-stakes business decisions.

Because RLHF rewards models for looking correct rather than being correct, LLMs naturally exhibit a bias toward overpromising and user flattery (demonstrated humorously by ChatGPT praising a series of fart sounds as 'eerie atmospheric music'). To bypass this limitation, businesses must transition from building conversational assistants to engineering true automation. Almeida criticizes the trend of using AI simply to write code faster—the 'just-in-time software' model—arguing that SaaS platforms have not evolved structurally since 2019. Instead of cheaper legacy software, the industry needs smarter, more expressive software capable of making reliable choices.

Almeida introduces TypeSafe, his stealth startup designed to rebuild the AI post-training stack for reliable, autonomous decision-making. Rejecting both human-preference optimization (RLHF) and pure rule/correctness optimization (RLVR), TypeSafe is pioneering a third paradigm focused on mainlining the immense compressed knowledge of pre-trained models into calibrated software actions.

## Chapters

### `00:12` — Introduction and OpenAI Background

Tiago Almeida introduces himself as an OpenAI veteran who co-authored GPT-4, ChatGPT, and InstructGPT. He explains why he critically challenges the limitations of the very algorithms he helped invent.

### `01:25` — The Great AI Divide

Almeida outlines the conflicting viewpoints in tech between those who believe AI is progressing exponentially and those who see it as an unproductive financial bubble, setting up his framework to explain this gap.

### `04:20` — Assistance vs. Automation

The speaker defines the split between tasks designed to keep a human in the loop (assistance) and those intended to run silently in the background (automation), arguing that today's AI is native only to the former.

### `05:52` — The Structural Flaws of RLHF

Almeida breaks down how RLHF works, proving that optimizing for human preference structurally encourages models to hallucinate, overpromise, and value user engagement over objective correctness.

### `09:01` — Reimagining Software for Automation

The discussion shifts to why SaaS architecture has stagnated since 2019. Almeida argues against the 'just-in-time software' paradigm, advocating instead for fundamentally smarter, more expressive software.

### `12:20` — Building TypeSafe

Almeida introduces his stealth-stage startup, TypeSafe, which aims to redesign the post-training stack from scratch to prioritize reliability, calibration, and automation.

### `13:54` — Audience Q&A and Technical Discussion

Almeida answers technical questions regarding reward model asymmetry, the limitations of pre-training, and how his approach differs from Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR).

## Notable Quotes

> "What makes me somewhat unique here is that I'm one of the few people at OpenAI who actually hates on chat GPT."
> — `01:18`

> "Today's AI, everything inherited from RLHF, is incredible at the human in the loop stuff, but not for automation tasks."
> — `05:17`

> "The main objective you're optimizing for is for human preference... No matter how wrong the models are, they will look right."
> — `07:20`

> "What you really want if you want automation is for it to just not give a shit about the humans and just do the task correctly in a calibrated way."
> — `08:01`
